meta.title: ACC Mock Exam — Set 1
meta.description: 60 scenario-based questions on the 2025 ICF Core Competencies, coaching boundaries, and Code of Ethics.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A division director pays for an employee's coaching and emails the coach asking which leadership topics the employee is addressing. What should the coach do?

options.text: Ask the employee for written permission to share a brief list of session topics.
Provide only broad developmental themes while keeping the employee's specific remarks private.
Decline to disclose session topics and invite the director to speak with the employee.
Send the director a summary of session topics since the organization funds the engagement.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance). Session content remains strictly confidential unless explicitly agreed otherwise in the coaching agreement, so declining disclosure and redirecting the sponsor to communicate directly with the client upholds privacy without pressuring the client. Option D is clearly wrong because funding the engagement does not grant a third-party sponsor access to session content. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A sounds consent-oriented, yet places organizational pressure on the employee to waive privacy after a superior requested information; Option B sounds protective by keeping specific remarks private, yet sharing even broad themes without prior authorization still breaches confidentiality.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client mentions months of exhaustion, trouble concentrating, and losing interest in hobbies, then asks how to rebuild motivation. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Validate their exhaustion and explore small daily routines that might restore energy.
Clarify coaching boundaries and encourage consulting a qualified mental health or medical professional.
Focus on manageable weekly wins first to see whether motivation improves over time.
Point out signs of clinical depression and outline steps to rebuild daily motivation.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice, Sub-competencies 1.06 and 1.07) and Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value). Months of exhaustion, concentration difficulties, and lost interest in hobbies suggest potential clinical or medical concerns beyond coaching scope; the coach clarifies coaching limits and encourages consulting a qualified specialist without diagnosing. Option D is clearly wrong because coaches are not qualified to identify clinical depression or prescribe recovery interventions. Options A and C are tricky distractors: both use supportive coaching language ('validate', 'explore', 'weekly wins'), yet treat potential clinical or medical symptoms as a routine habit gap and delay appropriate referral.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 7: Evokes Awareness
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client feels micromanaged at work and asks, 'Should I confront my boss or start looking for another job?' What is the BEST response?

options.text: Ask the client to compare the pros and cons of those two choices.
Ask why their boss might be micromanaging their daily work right now.
Advise the client to address the concern with their boss before resigning.
Ask what matters most to the client in this situation right now.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 Core Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Asking what matters most opens reflection on the client's underlying values, needs, and agency before narrowing down options. Option C is clearly wrong because it gives direct advice rather than facilitating client self-discovery. Options A and B are tricky distractors that look like open coaching questions: Option A accepts the client's forced binary dilemma and rushes into evaluating those two paths prematurely; Option B uses a 'why' question that pulls the client into speculating about their boss's motives instead of deepening their own awareness.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 1: Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A new client wants to start immediately and asks to review the written coaching agreement after the first session. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Confirm essential coaching agreement terms together before beginning the first coaching conversation.
Honor the client's urgency today and schedule ten minutes next week for logistics.
Summarize confidentiality briefly now and email the remaining terms to read after coaching.
Proceed straight into coaching since the client already verbally agreed to start working.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 1 (Agreements for Client and/or Sponsor Engagement). Coaches must co-create and confirm clear agreements covering the nature of coaching, confidentiality bounds, roles, responsibilities, fees, logistics, and termination before or at the initial session. Option D is clearly wrong because starting coaching without establishing the agreement omits essential ethical protections. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds client-led by accommodating urgency, yet leaves the client ungrounded on boundaries and expectations during Session 1; Option C sounds efficient by mentioning confidentiality, yet defers mutual confirmation of roles, logistics, and termination until after coaching has already occurred.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: An attorney sends a formal court subpoena requesting a coach's session notes for a client's workplace dispute. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Decline the request because ICF confidentiality standards protect private coaching session notes.
Consult legal counsel, notify the client if permitted, and disclose only mandated records.
Ask the client for written permission before taking action on the subpoena.
Forward the entire coaching file to the attorney promptly to comply legally.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance). Confidentiality does not create legal privilege against valid court mandates; consulting legal counsel verifies what disclosure is legally required, notifying the client when permitted preserves transparency, and disclosing only mandated records complies with the law. Option D is clearly wrong because sending the entire file without legal review or scope minimization risks unnecessary over-disclosure. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A rigidly misapplies ICF confidentiality as overriding valid legal mandates; Option C sounds respectful of client consent, yet compliance with a legal subpoena cannot be withheld pending client permission.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach plans to use an AI transcription and summary tool during online client sessions. What MUST the coach do first?

options.text: Use the AI tool only after configuring it to delete recordings automatically.
Mention in the welcome email that AI note-taking runs during video sessions.
Run the AI tool in the background to maintain thorough notes for continuity.
Secure the client's explicit informed consent after verifying platform data privacy safeguards.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2, Standard 2.5 (AI & Technology). Coaches must safeguard client privacy, verify compliance with data protection standards, and obtain explicit informed consent before capturing or processing client conversations with AI tools. Option C is clearly wrong because running an AI tool in the background without disclosure or consent violates confidentiality, trust, and Standard 2.5. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A takes a helpful privacy precaution (auto-deletion) yet still processes client data through AI without informing or getting consent from the client; Option B offers passive notice in an email rather than securing informed consent and an explicit opportunity to decline.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-engagement, a coach discovers during a session that the client's newly appointed business partner is the coach's sibling. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Disclose the family relationship openly and partner with the client on next steps.
End the coaching engagement promptly and offer referrals to avoid divided loyalty.
Acknowledge the relationship internally and maintain strict professional neutrality during coaching sessions.
Mention the coaching relationship to the sibling to establish shared ground rules.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest). When an actual or potential conflict of interest arises, the coach must disclose it transparently to the client and discuss together how to manage boundaries or transition to another coach if appropriate. Option D is clearly wrong because revealing that the client is in coaching to the sibling breaches confidentiality under Section 2. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds ethically decisive, yet rigidly terminates without partnering transparently with the client on options; Option C acknowledges the conflict privately while relying on internal neutrality instead of fulfilling the mandatory disclosure duty.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: An internal coach is assigned to coach a manager competing for the same promotion as the coach's close friend. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Disclose the friendship to the manager and let them decide whether to proceed.
Accept the assignment while keeping strict confidentiality and separating personal friendships from work.
Disclose the conflict of interest to the coaching sponsor and request reassignment.
Accept the assignment and discuss the promotion criteria privately with the friend.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest). Coaching a direct promotion competitor of a close friend creates an unmanageable conflict of interest and risks perceived bias; the internal coach protects both parties' privacy and coaching integrity by disclosing the conflict to the assigning sponsor and requesting reassignment. Option D is clearly wrong because sharing insider promotion insights or coaching alongside private advice to the friend exploits the dual relationship. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A sounds client-respecting, yet may expose the friend's private candidacy and pressures an employee assigned by the organization; Option B attempts silent compartmentalization rather than properly addressing an actual conflict of interest.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Two months after a coaching engagement ends, a former client invites the coach to co-found a joint consulting venture. What should the coach consider first?

options.text: Decline the offer because ICF ethics prohibit commercial partnerships with former clients.
Assess elapsed time and any residual power dynamics before entering a joint venture.
Accept the offer after establishing a formal written consulting agreement with clear roles.
Accept the partnership because ethical obligations toward the client ended with the contract.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest). Before entering a business or personal relationship with a former client, coaches must carefully assess elapsed time since coaching ended, residual power dynamics, potential vulnerability or exploitation, and role confusion. Option D is clearly wrong because ethical duties regarding confidentiality and residual power dynamics extend beyond contract completion. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A rigidly overstates the rule—ICF prohibits romantic intimacy with current clients, not all post-coaching commercial ventures after thoughtful assessment; Option C jumps to formal consulting paperwork without first evaluating residual power dynamics only two months after coaching ended.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After earning a major promotion, a client mails the coach a luxury watch as a thank-you gift. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Accept the watch graciously since the engagement is ending and refusing may offend.
Accept the watch and donate its equivalent monetary value to a local charity.
Keep the watch and credit its estimated value toward future coaching sessions.
Return the watch respectfully while explaining professional gift boundaries with warm appreciation.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest). Accepting gifts of significant monetary value compromises professional boundaries, objectivity, and equitable client relationships; acknowledging the client's gratitude while explaining gift boundaries and returning the watch preserves integrity and warmth. Option C is clearly wrong because keeping the gift and crediting its value toward future sessions creates an improper fee and bartering entanglement. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A rationalizes accepting an extravagant gift to avoid social awkwardness; Option B sounds altruistic by donating the value to charity, yet still accepts a high-value gift without upholding clear gift boundaries.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A startup founder asks a coach who previously served as a CTO to review their product roadmap and identify technical risks. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Examine the roadmap together and ask questions about technical gaps the coach notices.
Provide a brief risk assessment at the start, then return to regular coaching.
Explain that roadmap evaluation is consulting rather than coaching and discuss appropriate options.
Analyze the product roadmap thoroughly and deliver a written list of technical recommendations.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting). Using prior technical expertise to audit a product roadmap and flag risks is consulting, not coaching; the coach names this role distinction clearly and partners with the founder on how to proceed (such as exploring the founder's thinking via coaching or contracting separately for consulting/referral). Option D is clearly wrong because it performs full consulting work inside the coaching relationship. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A disguises expert critique inside 'questions' about technical gaps the coach noticed; Option B attempts a quick hybrid ('brief risk assessment') that still mixes consulting into coaching without re-contracting.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A prospective client currently sees a licensed therapist for anxiety and wants coaching to organize daily work priorities. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Establish distinct boundaries between coaching and therapy while creating a clear coaching agreement.
Decline the coaching request until the client finishes therapy and feels ready.
Require written clearance from the therapist before accepting the client for work coaching.
Agree to coach work priorities while also offering coping techniques for their anxiety.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy) and Code of Ethics Section 1. Coaching and therapy can coexist effectively when their purposes are distinct (future-focused work organization versus clinical anxiety treatment) and the coach explicitly establishes scope boundaries in the coaching agreement. Option D is clearly wrong because offering anxiety coping techniques crosses into therapy. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B rigidly misapplies scope boundaries by excluding anyone currently in therapy; Option C sounds clinically cautious, yet creates unnecessary gatekeeping and blurs coaching autonomy with medical clearance when the client seeks ordinary work-priority coaching.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Mentoring
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A newly promoted team lead asks the coach to share three mistakes the coach made early in leadership so they can avoid them. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Share one brief mistake as an example, then ask how that applies here.
Distinguish mentoring from coaching openly and ask what concerns them most right now.
Clarify that coaches avoid discussing personal history so sessions center solely on clients.
List three personal leadership mistakes and explain exactly how to prevent each one.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Mentoring) and Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Offering personal leadership stories as cautionary guidance is mentoring; distinguishing the roles politely and asking what concerns the client keeps the client's own context and insights at the center. Option D is clearly wrong because it slips entirely into prescriptive mentoring. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A compromises by offering 'just one brief mistake', which still centers the coach's narrative instead of the client's reality; Option C uses coaching language ('center solely on clients') yet rigidly shuts down the request without naming the mentoring distinction or inviting exploration.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Management
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client's manager asks the coach to observe a team meeting and evaluate the client's executive presence for an upcoming appraisal. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Ask the client whether they feel comfortable having the coach evaluate their meeting.
Observe the meeting silently and share only strengths observed with the client's manager.
Decline the evaluation request because coaching is non-evaluative and distinct from management appraisal.
Attend the team meeting and send the manager a written executive presence rating.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Management) and Code of Ethics Sections 2 and 3. Assessing performance for a formal appraisal is a management function incompatible with the confidential, non-judgmental coaching partnership; the coach declines clearly while clarifying the role boundary. Option D is clearly wrong because submitting an appraisal rating acts directly as a manager/evaluator. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A sounds collaborative, yet places subtle pressure on the client to consent to their coach judging them for an appraisal; Option B tries to soften the breach by reporting 'only strengths', yet still performs an evaluation for management.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Friendship
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client repeatedly spends the first half of sessions chatting about weekend trips, explaining that casual conversation helps them unwind. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Allow the casual chatting to continue because informal warmth builds psychological safety.
Remind the client that coaching requires staying focused solely on their agreed goals.
Share stories about the coach's own weekend plans to strengthen mutual rapport.
Acknowledge their desire to unwind while partnering to establish purposeful session boundaries.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Friendship) and Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements). Coaching differs from friendship by maintaining purposeful focus toward client goals; acknowledging the client's desire to unwind while partnering on clear, purposeful session boundaries preserves trust and value. Option C is clearly wrong because trading personal weekend stories shifts the relationship into social friendship. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A misinterprets psychological safety as accommodating half-session social banter; Option B sounds disciplined, yet lectures unilaterally without acknowledging the client's transition need or partnering on structure.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Medical Advice
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client mentions taking unprescribed sleeping pills every night and asks the coach to help build morning energy habits. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Clarify coaching limits around medical matters and encourage consulting a qualified healthcare professional.
Focus solely on morning energy routines since the client chose that coaching topic.
Explore which morning habits have previously helped them feel alert despite poor sleep.
Advise the client to stop taking those pills and switch to herbal melatonin.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Medical Advice) and Code of Ethics Section 4. Regular unprescribed use of sleep medication presents a medical risk directly tied to morning energy; the coach recognizes competence limits, refrains from medical advice, and encourages consulting a qualified healthcare professional. Option D is clearly wrong because instructing the client to stop pills and recommending supplements constitutes unauthorized medical advice. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B invokes 'client choice' to overlook an obvious health red flag; Option C uses neutral coaching inquiry ('explore which morning habits') while sidestepping the unsafe medical self-medication practice.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Training
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client asks the coach to spend the next two sessions teaching a structured one-on-one feedback model step by step. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Teach the feedback model briefly, then coach the client on applying each step.
Clarify that ICF coaches cannot provide training and redirect toward their feedback goals.
Distinguish training from coaching openly and agree whether to coach or contract separately.
Prepare training slides and deliver the full feedback curriculum over the next two sessions.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Training) and Code of Ethics Section 1. Step-by-step curriculum instruction is training rather than coaching; the coach clarifies the distinction transparently and partners with the client either to explore their feedback challenges via coaching or to establish a separate training arrangement. Option D is clearly wrong because it converts contracted coaching sessions directly into structured training delivery. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A quietly blends brief training into coaching without re-contracting; Option B rigidly misstates ICF ethics by claiming coaches can never offer training even under a separate agreement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client plans to leave a stable role for an unproven startup, which the coach privately views as unwise. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Ask questions focused on startup failure rates to help the client think realistically.
Set aside the internal doubt silently to remain curious about the client's perspective.
Share the private concern honestly so the coach remains transparent about potential career risks.
Advise the client to wait at least a year until the startup proves profitable.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 Core Competency 2 (Embodies a Coaching Mindset, including 2.09 nurturing openness and curiosity and 2.10 awareness of how the coach's thoughts influence the client). Maintaining a client-centered mindset means recognizing internal judgment without attachment, setting aside bias, and staying genuinely curious about the client's perspective. Option D is clearly wrong because it directly dictates the client's career timeline. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A wraps the coach's skepticism inside seemingly helpful 'realistic' questions that steer the client away from their choice; Option C mistakes sharing private personal risk judgments for helpful transparency, imposing the coach's values onto the client's decision.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A corporate sponsor sets three performance KPIs at kickoff, yet in Session 1 the client asks to focus on work-life boundaries instead. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Acknowledge their boundary concern, then gently steer the session back toward the sponsor's KPIs.
Set aside the sponsor's KPIs since coaching follows whatever agenda the client chooses.
Inform the sponsor promptly that the client refuses to work on agreed KPIs.
Explore the boundary focus in relation to KPIs and revisit agreements as needed.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 Core Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements, including 3.12 revisiting the agreement as needed). In sponsored engagements, the coach partners with both the client and stakeholders: exploring the client's immediate focus on boundaries, examining how sustainable boundaries relate to overall KPIs, and revisiting the multi-party agreement transparently if direction shifts. Option C is clearly wrong because it breaches confidentiality and reports on the client defensively. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A gives polite empathy before forcing the sponsor's agenda over the client's autonomy; Option B honors client autonomy yet ignores the coach's responsibility to honor or transparently renegotiate stakeholder agreements.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 8: Facilitates Client Growth
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client arrives at their fifth coaching session apologizing repeatedly for missing two consecutive self-assigned deadlines. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Acknowledge their candor and explore what got in the way or needs adjusting.
Reassure them warmly and co-create one smaller deadline to rebuild momentum today.
Normalize occasional missed deadlines warmly and ask what priority feels most urgent today.
Remind the client that consistent follow-through is essential for coaching value to occur.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 8 (Facilitates Client Growth). Client-owned accountability relies on non-judgmental exploration of setbacks to uncover obstacles, competing priorities, or misaligned goals so the client can adjust meaningfully. Option D is clearly wrong because lecturing about follow-through evokes shame and undermines psychological safety. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds encouraging and action-oriented, yet rushes into setting a new deadline without examining what derailed the previous two; Option C sounds warm and validating, yet bypasses a valuable learning and self-accountability conversation by shifting to another priority.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 1: Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Midway through a six-month prepaid coaching package, a client says coaching feels unhelpful and wants to stop immediately. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Explore what feels unhelpful and suggest trying two more sessions before stopping.
Respect the client's decision to stop and follow the agreed termination terms.
Ask what expectations went unmet before deciding whether to pause the contract.
Remind the client that the package is prepaid and keep sessions scheduled.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 1 (Agreements for Client and/or Sponsor Engagement, Standard 1.2), which requires coaches to respect any party's right to terminate coaching at any point for any reason, subject to the provisions of the agreement. Honoring the client's decision to stop while applying the pre-agreed termination and refund terms protects both client autonomy and contractual integrity. Option D is clearly wrong because it refuses the client's right to terminate solely because fees were prepaid. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds curious and supportive, yet subtly pressures the client to remain in two more unwanted sessions instead of honoring their immediate decision; Option C sounds reflective, yet makes termination conditional on a coach-approved pause rather than respecting the client's unconditional right to end the engagement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client's spouse emails the coach asking whether the client is still attending sessions, noting the client seems withdrawn at home. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Reassure the spouse that everything looks fine without sharing any session content.
Promise to check with the client before confirming whether sessions are continuing.
Confirm the client's recent attendance and encourage the spouse to talk directly.
Decline to confirm whether a coaching relationship exists or share any client information.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1 and 2.2), which obligate coaches to maintain the strictest level of confidentiality with all client information unless disclosure is explicitly agreed upon or legally required. Even confirming whether a person is an active client breaches confidentiality when no prior consent exists, and there is no stated threat of imminent harm. Option C is clearly wrong because confirming attendance directly reveals confidential relationship status and gives unsolicited advice to a third party. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A withholds session topics yet still implies an active coaching relationship while offering false reassurance; Option B sounds respectful of client autonomy, yet promising to check with the client already confirms the coaching relationship and places pressure on the client.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach plans to publish an anonymized case study in a niche industry journal featuring distinctive details of a client's turnaround project. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Publish the article as drafted because the client's real name was removed.
Omit the company name and publish only positive outcomes from the engagement.
Obtain the client's explicit informed consent before submitting the article for publication.
Email the draft to the client and publish it unless they raise objections.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.1 and 2.2), which require strict protection of client privacy and explicit agreement before disclosing identifiable client information. When distinctive project details in a niche publication could expose a client's identity, simple anonymization is insufficient and explicit informed consent is required prior to submission. Option A is clearly wrong because removing only the client's name fails to prevent identification. Options B and D are tricky distractors: Option B sounds benign because it removes the company name and shares only flattering results, yet confidentiality applies regardless of whether disclosures are positive; Option D sounds courteous, yet relies on passive opt-out silence rather than affirmative informed consent.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 2: Confidentiality & Legal Compliance
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach records virtual sessions and stores the files on an unencrypted personal cloud drive shared with a virtual assistant. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Transfer recordings to encrypted private storage and remove the assistant's folder access.
Label the recording files with client initials instead of full names for privacy.
Have the virtual assistant sign a formal confidentiality agreement to protect client privacy.
Leave the files in the folder since the video platform uses encryption.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 2 (Confidentiality and Legal Compliance, Standards 2.4 and 2.5), which require coaches to maintain, store, and dispose of electronic records in a manner promoting confidentiality, security, and privacy. Moving files to encrypted private storage and revoking third-party folder access directly resolves both vulnerabilities. Option D is clearly wrong because live video platform encryption does not protect stored files afterward. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B uses initials as a superficial privacy gesture while leaving full recordings unencrypted and accessible; Option C relies on a staff non-disclosure agreement, which sounds professional yet neither secures unencrypted storage nor justifies unrestricted third-party access to private sessions.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 3: Professional Conduct & Conflicts of Interest
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A prospective client offers to redesign a coach's website in exchange for six coaching sessions instead of paying fees. How should the coach respond?

options.text: Decline the offer because ICF ethics prohibit bartering coaching for other services.
Co-create transparent written terms addressing dual-role conflicts before starting the exchange.
Accept the exchange once both parties verbally agree the work feels equal.
Require the completed website first before scheduling any coaching sessions together.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest, Standards 3.1 and 3.2) and Section 1 (Standard 1.1). The ICF Code does not prohibit bartering; instead, coaches must openly examine overlapping dual-role implications (client and vendor), avoid conflicts of interest or exploitation, comply with applicable tax laws, and establish transparent, equitable agreements before starting. Option D is clearly wrong because demanding full delivery upfront creates an unbalanced power dynamic and leverage over the coaching relationship. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A rigidly misapplies the Code by falsely claiming bartering is banned outright; Option C focuses only on perceived equal value while skipping formal written terms and dual-role conflict management.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 4: Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client repeatedly asks the coach to decide their next career move, saying the coach knows best. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Acknowledge their request and explore two clear career paths they could choose.
Recommend the safest career path since the client explicitly requested expert guidance.
Close the coaching engagement because the client avoids taking ownership of choices.
Address the power dynamic openly and reaffirm the client's ownership of decisions.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value, Standards 4.2 and 4.3) and Core Competency 2 (2.01). When client idealization creates an unhealthy power imbalance, the coach must notice the shift in how coaching value is received, surface the power dynamic transparently, avoid fostering dependency, and restore client decision-making autonomy. Option B is clearly wrong because acting as an expert decision-maker directly violates coaching boundaries and deepens dependence. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A uses supportive language ('acknowledge', 'explore'), yet still generates options for the client to satisfy their idealization; Option C rigidly over-corrects by terminating the engagement before addressing the dynamic and re-establishing partnership.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 4: Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach accepts a pro bono client and considers cutting their session length during a busy period with paying clients. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Uphold the same committed session quality and duration regardless of client payment.
Shorten the sessions briefly while offering concise email check-ins as fair compensation.
Invite the pro bono client to shift to briefer sessions until workloads ease.
Shorten the pro bono sessions to prioritize paying client engagements during peak weeks.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value) and Section 1 (Agreements, Standard 1.1). ICF professionals must uphold equal quality, rigor, and reliability across all engagements regardless of fee structure, including pro bono coaching, and honor agreed session parameters. Option D is clearly wrong because unilaterally reducing pro bono session length to favor paying clients violates consistent value and agreed commitments. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B tries to look fair by substituting email check-ins, yet still downgrades the agreed coaching service because the client is not paying; Option C appears polite and collaborative ('invite'), yet pressures a pro bono client to accept reduced value during busy periods.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After completing an ICF-accredited training program, a coach awaiting their ACC exam results lists "ICF-certified coach" on LinkedIn. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Retain the title because graduating from an accredited program grants certification.
Keep the title "ICF-certified coach" and add "ACC exam pending" alongside it.
Remove the premature certification claim by stating completed ICF-accredited training accurately instead.
Change the headline to "ICF Associate Coach" until the official badge arrives.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 5 (Professional Integrity and Accountability, Standards 5.1 and 5.2), which mandate true and accurate representation of coaching qualifications, training, certifications, and ICF credentials. Until the credentialing process is formally completed and awarded, the coach may truthfully cite completed accredited training but must not claim ICF certification or credentialed status. Option A is clearly wrong because graduating from an accredited training program is distinct from holding an ICF credential. Options B and D are tricky distractors: Option B looks transparent with a qualifier, yet still displays the inaccurate "ICF-certified coach" claim; Option D drops the word "certified" yet creates a misleading headline closely mimicking the protected Associate Certified Coach (ACC) title.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach notices that a fellow ICF member's website promises prospective clients "a promotion within 90 days or a full refund." What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Take no action because refund policies remain each coach's private business choice.
Address the guarantee constructively with the colleague and contact ICF if unresolved.
Warn shared networking groups privately so prospective clients avoid misleading marketing claims.
Support the colleague's approach since offering a full refund ensures client fairness.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 5 (Professional Integrity and Accountability, Standards 5.2 and 5.3). Standard 5.2 requires true, accurate statements about coaching and its potential value—coaches cannot guarantee external outcomes like a promotion—and ICF professionals uphold accountability by addressing suspected breaches constructively with peers and using the ICF Ethical Conduct Review process when unresolved. Option D is clearly wrong because a refund policy never legitimizes guaranteeing outcomes outside coaching's control. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A rationalizes inaction as respecting business autonomy, overlooking professional accountability; Option C appears protective of prospective clients, yet spreads informal reputational warnings instead of engaging the colleague directly or using ICF's formal accountability channels.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Code of Ethics Section 5: Professional Integrity & Accountability
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach finds another practitioner's copyrighted leadership framework online and wants to include it on client worksheets. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Include the diagram freely because using it privately with clients is noncommercial.
Print the worksheet with a footnote citing the author without requesting permission.
Redesign the visual layout and add a note crediting its original inspiration.
Secure the creator's permission with proper attribution before distributing the copyrighted framework.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 5 (Professional Integrity and Accountability) and its Intellectual Property obligations, which require ICF professionals to respect and honor others' intellectual property and only claim ownership of their own work. Distributing a copyrighted model requires securing the owner's authorization or license alongside proper attribution. Option A is clearly wrong because client worksheets used in coaching practice are still covered by copyright protections. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B assumes academic-style citation alone permits reproducing protected material without consent; Option C sounds creative and respectful by crediting inspiration while altering the layout, yet still uses protected intellectual property without permission.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client whose parent died three weeks ago feels periodic grief, yet asks to focus on leading their team through a merger. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Proceed with coaching on the leadership goal while monitoring if referral becomes appropriate.
Refer the client to a grief counselor and pause coaching until grief subsides.
Dedicate the session to exploring unresolved grief feelings before discussing workplace leadership.
Advise the client to set personal sadness aside during upcoming leadership coaching.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice, Sub-competencies 1.06 and 1.07), which require distinguishing coaching from psychotherapy and referring when appropriate. Periodic sadness three weeks after a bereavement is normal grief, not clinical impairment; when the client remains functional and seeks forward-looking leadership coaching, partnering on that goal while staying attentive to emerging support needs respects client agency. Option D is clearly wrong because telling the client to suppress sadness is directive and dismisses their humanity (Competency 4). Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B rigidly misapplies referral rules by pathologizing normal grief; Option C sounds compassionate, yet overrides the client's chosen leadership agenda to steer into grief processing.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During a session, a client asks the coach which project management software works best for distributed engineering teams. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Recommend two top platforms and explain how distributed teams usually configure them.
Ask if standard agile platforms could resolve their distributed coordination challenges quickly.
Explore what criteria matter most for the team's workflow and selection process.
Decline to discuss software choices and redirect the session toward leadership mindset.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice, Sub-competency 1.06) and Core Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Rather than stepping into an IT consulting role by recommending software, the coach maintains role clarity and partners with the client to surface their own criteria, workflow priorities, and evaluation plan. Option A is clearly wrong because recommending platforms and configurations shifts directly into consulting. Options B and D are tricky distractors: Option B frames disguised consulting advice as a leading question pointing toward standard agile software; Option D rigidly over-corrects by refusing to coach around a legitimate operational decision, shutting down a topic that matters to the client.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Medical Advice
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: During a wellness coaching session, a client asks whether they can stop taking blood-pressure medication now that they exercise daily. What MUST the coach do?

options.text: Explore how confident the client feels about managing blood pressure through exercise.
Clarify that medication changes lie outside coaching scope and refer to their doctor.
Suggest tapering the dose gradually while tracking daily readings over two weeks.
Note that exercise helps many people reduce doses, though caution remains important.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice, Sub-competencies 1.06 and 1.07) and Code of Ethics Section 4 (Standard 4.1). Adjusting prescribed medication requires licensed medical judgment outside the scope of coaching, so the coach must state that boundary clearly and direct the client to consult their prescribing physician. Option C is clearly wrong because advising a tapering schedule constitutes dangerous, unlicensed medical guidance. Options A and D are tricky distractors: Option A sounds like classic open-ended coaching, yet fails to establish the medical scope boundary and implicitly treats stopping prescriptions as a coaching decision; Option D adds a cautious disclaimer while still offering implied medical commentary on dose reduction.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Advocacy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client feels treated unfairly by HR and asks the coach to speak with HR on their behalf to explain their stress. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Offer to meet with HR only if the client signs written consent first.
Email HR privately to share the client's stress levels and request accommodations.
Explore whether the client wants their manager to speak with HR instead.
Decline to advocate with HR and explore how the client wants to respond.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice, Sub-competency 1.06) and Core Competency 2 (2.01). Coaching empowers clients to speak and act for themselves rather than having the coach act as an advocate, spokesperson, or mediator with third parties such as HR. Option B is clearly wrong because contacting HR unilaterally breaches confidentiality and violates role boundaries. Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A assumes written consent solves the dilemma, overlooking that advocating on the client's behalf compromises coaching neutrality and client agency even with consent; Option C uses exploratory phrasing yet steers the client with disguised advice toward finding another intermediary instead of exploring the client's own voice and choices.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach notices irritation rising whenever a client speaks dismissively about junior staff, recalling a former boss. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Ground oneself silently upon noticing the personal trigger to remain genuinely curious.
Share the irritation openly and ask how junior staff might feel hearing that.
End the coaching engagement afterward because personal reactions compromise coaching neutrality.
Challenge the client's attitude directly so they adopt more respectful leadership habits.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 2 (Embodies a Coaching Mindset, including 2.06 managing emotions to stay grounded, 2.09 nurturing curiosity, and 2.10 remaining aware of how one's thoughts and behaviors influence the client). Self-regulating an emotional trigger in real time keeps the space client-centered, and the coach can process the reaction later through reflective practice or coaching supervision (2.03, 2.08). Option D is clearly wrong because imposing corrective judgment acts directly on the coach's bias. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B mimics sharing observations without attachment, yet projects unresolved personal irritation into a leading question; Option C over-corrects by abandoning the engagement instead of managing the trigger through self-awareness and supervision.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 2: Embodies a Coaching Mindset
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After three emotionally intense sessions back-to-back, a coach feels mentally depleted ten minutes before the next client call. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Push through the exhaustion and rely on routine coaching questions to finish.
Tell the client about the fatigue and ask for a lighter topic.
Practice intentional grounding to restore well-being, or reschedule if focus stays impaired.
Spend the ten minutes studying past session notes to compensate for fatigue.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 2, Sub-competency 2.07 ("Maintains emotional, physical, and mental well-being in preparation for, throughout, and following each session") and Code of Ethics Standard 4.2. Taking intentional steps to reset presence before the session—or responsibly rescheduling if capacity remains impaired—protects both coach well-being and consistent service quality. Option A is clearly wrong because powering through depleted attention compromises presence and client care. Options B and D are tricky distractors: Option B sounds candid, yet places the coach's self-care burden onto the client and restricts the client's session agenda; Option D looks conscientious, yet reviewing detailed notes increases mental strain instead of restoring emotional and cognitive readiness.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Fifteen minutes into a time-management session, a client sighs and admits their real worry is a rumored company restructuring. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Stay with time management because changing topics mid-session weakens the original plan.
Ask which restructuring rumors worry them most to understand the wider context.
Suggest prioritizing urgent tasks today so restructuring uncertainty feels less overwhelming.
Acknowledge the worry and ask whether they want to shift today's focus.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 Core Competency 3, Sub-competency 3.12 ("Revisits the coaching agreement when necessary to ensure the coaching approach is meeting the client's needs"). When a client reveals a deeper concern mid-session, partnering to confirm whether to continue the original topic or re-contract around what matters most preserves both alignment and client ownership. Option C is clearly wrong because it bypasses the client's emerging concern with prescriptive task advice. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A prioritizes sticking to the initial plan over serving the client's real-time need; Option B sounds curious and context-gathering, yet dives straight into organizational details without first partnering to reset the session agreement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client hesitates to challenge a senior executive, explaining that questioning elders openly feels deeply disrespectful in their culture. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Ask how adopting more direct workplace norms might help them advance faster.
Respect their cultural perspective and explore ways to engage that feel authentic.
Acknowledge that cultural discomfort is natural and explore a less stressful topic.
Explain that modern leadership requires speaking up openly regardless of cultural background.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 Core Competency 4 (Cultivates Trust and Safety), which calls on coaches to understand the client within their context—including identity, values, and cultural beliefs—and demonstrate genuine respect while supporting candid expression. Honoring the client's cultural value and exploring authentic options enables growth without forcing assimilation. Option D is clearly wrong because lecturing the client to override their cultural values breaks trust and cultural humility (Competency 1.02). Options A and C are tricky distractors: Option A sounds curious, yet embeds a leading push toward Western directness; Option C sounds warm and validating ('acknowledge', 'explore'), yet avoids exploring culturally congruent pathways forward by shifting away from the client's challenge.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client admits a painful leadership mistake they feel ashamed of and watches the coach closely for signs of disapproval. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Receive their disclosure calmly and acknowledge their openness in sharing something difficult.
Reassure them that all leaders make mistakes and urge them not to worry.
Acknowledge the mistake briefly and ask what corrective step they will take next.
Ask why they chose that approach when the leadership risks seemed clear.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 Core Competency 4 (Cultivates Trust and Safety), which emphasizes creating a supportive, nonjudgmental environment where clients can express difficult feelings freely and acknowledging their courage and transparency. Calmly holding space without judgment or rescuing builds genuine psychological safety. Option D is clearly wrong because asking a judgmental "why" question reinforces shame and defensiveness. Options B and C are tricky distractors: Option B sounds empathetic and comforting, yet slips into rescuing and minimizing the client's emotion rather than letting them sit with and learn from it; Option C sounds action-oriented, yet rushes into Competency 8 problem-solving before safety and awareness are established.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 5: Maintains Presence
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A coach planned a structured values exercise, yet the client arrives visibly shaken by a board confrontation. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Suggest doing the prepared values exercise first to help restore emotional balance.
Offer to reschedule the session so the client can recover from the shock.
Set aside the planned exercise and stay grounded with what is emerging now.
Walk through the confrontation step by step to determine who was at fault.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 Core Competency 5 (Maintains Presence, including 5.03 tracking what is emerging for self and client in the present moment, working confidently with strong emotions, and adapting without attachment to a plan). Meeting the shaken client calmly in the moment and setting aside the prepared exercise keeps coaching centered on the client's lived reality. Option D is clearly wrong because conducting a fault-finding review shifts out of coaching presence into judgmental investigation. Options A and B are tricky distractors: Option A rationalizes keeping the coach's agenda as emotionally stabilizing, showing attachment to preparation; Option B appears considerate of distress, yet retreats out of discomfort with strong emotion instead of holding steady presence.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: While discussing ongoing friction with their manager, a client asks whether the manager's behavior sounds like a personality disorder. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Offer informal thoughts on traits linked to personality disorders based on the client's description.
Pause the coaching engagement and refer the client to a licensed mental health professional.
Ask which specific manager behaviors lead the client to consider a clinical personality label.
Explain that clinical assessment lies outside coaching before inviting the client's next focus.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy) and the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value), which require coaches to recognize scope limits and distinguish coaching from clinical assessment or therapy. Clarifying that diagnosing mental health conditions is outside coaching and returning focus to the client's path forward maintains ethical boundaries and client agency. Option A is clearly wrong because offering informal diagnostic speculation about a third party violates competence and scope boundaries. Option B is a tricky distractor representing rigid over-correction: asking about a manager's behavior does not indicate the client needs therapy or require pausing coaching. Option C is a tricky distractor that sounds like open coaching curiosity, yet pulls the session into evaluating evidence for a clinical diagnosis rather than maintaining the boundary.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Over several sessions, a client repeatedly steers away from leadership goals to process ongoing pain from a past divorce. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Guide the client through processing the emotional pain of the divorce to help them heal.
Name the recurring pattern while distinguishing coaching from therapy and discussing referral options.
Follow the client's lead and explore how the divorce continues shaping their daily feelings.
Clarify the coaching agreement and redirect each conversation back to their leadership goals.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Therapy) and the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value). When a client persistently uses coaching to process ongoing emotional pain from a past divorce rather than forward-looking goals, the coach transparently names the pattern, clarifies the distinction between coaching and therapy, and discusses referral support. Option A is clearly wrong because guiding emotional divorce healing crosses directly into therapy. Option C is a tricky distractor that misapplies 'following the client's lead' and empathy to indulge ongoing therapeutic processing outside coaching scope. Option D is a tricky distractor that invokes Competency 3's coaching agreement mechanically while ignoring the ethical responsibility to address the recurring pattern and offer appropriate referral support.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Overwhelmed by a difficult staffing decision, a client asks the coach to draft three versions of an employee termination email. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Clarify that drafting workplace emails lies outside coaching before exploring their communication approach.
Offer a general termination outline so the client can supply the specific details afterward.
Write the three email drafts during the session so the client can select one.
Ask how delegating the termination email to human resources could reduce their current stress.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting) and the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Section 4 (Commitment to Delivering Consistent Value). Drafting workplace communications is operational consulting rather than coaching; clarifying that writing emails falls outside coaching while exploring the client's own communication approach preserves client ownership. Option C is clearly wrong because producing the email drafts directly violates the Coaching vs. Consulting boundary. Option B is a tricky distractor that feels supportive and collaborative, yet still supplies consulting work-product rather than coaching the client's thinking. Option D is a tricky distractor that uses an open-sounding question to embed disguised advice ('delegate to HR') while sidestepping the required clarification of the coaching role.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A newly promoted VP asks their coach, who also consults in finance, to spend half of each session giving financial advice. How MUST the coach respond?

options.text: Dedicate half of every session to financial advice since the VP requested expert guidance.
State clearly at each session midpoint when shifting from coaching into financial consulting.
Distinguish coaching from consulting openly and keep any consulting engagement structurally separate.
End the coaching relationship because dual expertise creates an unavoidable ethical conflict of interest.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Consulting) and the 2025 ICF Code of Ethics Sections 1 (Agreements) and 3 (Professional Conduct and Conflicts of Interest). Coaches must clearly distinguish coaching from consulting and avoid blending both services inside the same session, keeping any consulting work structurally separate under distinct agreements or referrals. Option A is clearly wrong because giving ongoing expert advice inside coaching sessions violates role boundaries just because the client asked. Option B is a tricky distractor that sounds transparent, yet routinely splitting each coaching session in half blurs role boundaries, fosters expert dependency, and creates dual-role confusion without separate agreements. Option D is a tricky distractor representing rigid over-correction: possessing consulting expertise does not require ending coaching when clear structural boundaries can be maintained.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 1: Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Training
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After a promotion, a client realizes they lack spreadsheet skills and asks the coach to walk them through pivot tables. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Spend the rest of the session teaching the client how to build pivot tables.
Explain that technical instruction falls outside coaching and explore how they will learn it.
Suggest a specific spreadsheet training course and ask how quickly the client can finish it.
Clarify that technical training lies outside coaching and pause sessions until instruction concludes.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 1 (Demonstrates Ethical Practice — Coaching vs. Training) and Competency 8 (Facilitates Client Growth). Teaching technical software tools is training rather than coaching; the coach explains that boundary and partners with the client to explore their own options for acquiring the skill. Option A is clearly wrong because delivering step-by-step software instruction turns the session into training without agreement. Option C is a tricky distractor that sounds encouraging and accountability-focused, yet prescribes a specific solution ('suggest a specific course') while failing to clarify the Coaching vs. Training distinction. Option D is a tricky distractor representing rigid over-correction: a client needing technical upskilling can still be coached around transition goals and learning strategies without pausing the engagement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client opens the session by listing four unrelated crises from that morning and says, "I don't even know where to start." What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Select the most urgent crisis and ask the client to walk through the background.
Invite the client to describe each of the four crises briefly so nothing is overlooked.
Ask which immediate action step the client wants to commit to before the session ends.
Acknowledge the hectic morning and ask what the client most wants from today's session.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements). When a client arrives scattered across multiple crises, the coach partners with the client to establish a clear session agreement by acknowledging their experience and inviting them to define the most valuable focus and outcome for the session. Option A is clearly wrong because the coach unilaterally selects the agenda rather than honoring client choice. Option B is a tricky distractor that sounds organized and attentive, yet pulls the session into storytelling across four issues before agreeing on what matters most to work on. Option C is a tricky distractor that rushes prematurely into Competency 8 action planning before the client has established the session focus under Competency 3.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 3: Establishes and Maintains Agreements
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Halfway through a twelve-session agreement, a client earns the promotion they wanted, and recent sessions have felt unfocused. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Name what has shifted transparently to partner with the client on overall goals.
Propose new executive stretch goals for the remaining sessions to maintain steady forward momentum.
Suggest ending the engagement early because the client already achieved their initial promotion goal.
Ask at the next session which immediate daily task the client wants to address.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 3 (Establishes and Maintains Agreements, specifically Sub-competency 3.12: revisiting the coaching agreement when needed to ensure coaching meets the client's needs). Naming the shift transparently and partnering to redefine overall coaching goals ensures the engagement either aligns around meaningful new priorities or transitions purposefully. Option B is clearly wrong because the coach invents and imposes new goals instead of partnering with the client. Option C is a tricky distractor representing rigid over-correction: assuming coaching must end early bypasses exploring whether new leadership transition goals have emerged. Option D is a tricky distractor that sounds client-led at the single-session level, yet fails to address the broader engagement drift by redefining the overall coaching agreement.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 4: Cultivates Trust and Safety
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-session, a client abruptly says, "I get the sense you think I'm making excuses for staying in this job too long." What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Explain that the coach was only asking neutral questions and holds no personal judgment.
Explore whether part of them worries they have been making excuses for staying.
Thank the client for speaking candidly and explore what gave them that impression now.
Apologize briefly for any unintended tone and redirect back toward their career action plan.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 4 (Cultivates Trust and Safety) and Competency 2 (Embodies a Coaching Mindset). Welcoming candid feedback non-defensively and curiously exploring what contributed to the client's perception strengthens psychological safety and mutual trust. Option A is clearly wrong because defending the coach's intent dismisses the client's lived experience in the moment. Option B is a tricky distractor that uses reflective inquiry ('explore'), yet deflects relational feedback onto the client's psyche before tending to safety and trust. Option D is a tricky distractor that sounds polite and task-focused, yet papers over a potential relational rupture without allowing open dialogue about what occurred.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 5: Maintains Presence
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: After voicing a surprising realization, a client suddenly stops speaking and stares thoughtfully at their desk for ten seconds. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Summarize the client's realization promptly to keep momentum flowing rather than letting silence linger.
Hold grounded silence to give the client unhurried space with that realization.
Ask gently whether the client would like to unpack that realization out loud now.
Tell the client gently to take all the time they need before speaking again.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 5 (Maintains Presence), which emphasizes being comfortable with silence and staying grounded in the present moment so the client can process deeply. Holding ten seconds of thoughtful silence without rushing allows insight to unfold naturally. Option A is clearly wrong because summarizing promptly interrupts the client's active reflection to manage pace. Option C is a tricky distractor that uses gentle, supportive phrasing, yet breaks a productive silence by nudging the client to talk out loud before they finish processing. Option D is a tricky distractor that sounds accommodating and kind, yet paradoxically disrupts the client's internal silence by speaking into it.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 5: Maintains Presence
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: Mid-session, a coach senses an intuitive hunch that the client may be sidestepping a key stakeholder conflict. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Point out that the client is avoiding a key conflict and ask why that happens.
Withhold the intuition so the coach avoids introducing outside assumptions into the conversation.
Ask how resolving an unspoken stakeholder conflict could move the client closer to their goal.
Offer the hunch tentatively and invite the client to confirm, adjust, or set it aside.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 5 (Maintains Presence, including Sub-competency 5.03: tracking what is emerging for self and client in the present moment) and Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Sharing an emerging hunch lightly without attachment honors the client as the authority who can accept, reshape, or discard it. Option A is clearly wrong because stating the hunch as objective truth confronts the client and uses a judgmental 'why' question. Option B is a tricky distractor representing rigid over-correction: suppressing all intuitive observations deprives the client of potentially valuable awareness when shared without attachment. Option C is a tricky distractor that embeds an unverified assumption as a leading question rather than testing the hunch transparently.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 6: Listens Actively
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client enthusiastically says they are thrilled about an overseas transfer while gripping their hands tightly and frowning. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Notice aloud their excited words alongside their gripping hands to invite personal reflection.
Acknowledge that they seem anxious beneath the excitement and explore what worries them most.
Match the client's upbeat energy and ask how they want to celebrate the upcoming move.
Ask whether the client genuinely wants the transfer given how hesitant their expression looks.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option A is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 6 (Listens Actively), which calls on the coach to attend to words, tone, energy, and non-verbal cues and reflect them succinctly without adding the coach's interpretation. Mirroring their spoken excitement alongside the observable gripping hands invites the client to make their own meaning. Option C is clearly wrong because ignoring glaring non-verbal incongruence misses critical data and colludes with surface excitement. Option B is a tricky distractor that sounds empathetic, yet inserts the coach's interpretation ('anxious', 'worries') rather than sharing neutral observations. Option D is a tricky distractor because it also interprets the expression ('hesitant') and poses a closed, questioning prompt about authenticity.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 6: Listens Actively
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: While describing their workload, a client repeats the phrase, "I have to carry everyone on my back" three times. What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Recommend setting firmer workload boundaries so the client stops doing work for their coworkers.
Reflect that they sound resentful toward unreliable coworkers and ask what frustrates them most.
Reflect their repeated phrase "carry everyone on my back" and ask what that means.
Ask why the client originally took on so much responsibility across the wider team.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option C is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 6 (Listens Actively) and Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). Noticing repeated language and mirroring the client's exact metaphor without adding coach interpretation deepens self-awareness directly through the client's worldview. Option A is clearly wrong because giving direct advice and labeling the client's behavior bypasses active listening and client autonomy. Option B is a tricky distractor that sounds emotionally observant, yet replaces the client's language with the coach's assumptions ('resentful', 'unreliable coworkers'). Option D is a tricky distractor that sounds curious about root causes, yet overlooks the client's vivid present metaphor and pulls backward into 'why' justification.

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 6: Listens Actively
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client spends several minutes recounting tangled department politics with shifting names and competing priorities. What is the BEST action for the coach?

options.text: Ask the client to detail each coworker's background so every political dynamic becomes clear.
Summarize the core threads succinctly before asking what matters most to address.
Gently pause the client to remind them of the time remaining and session goal.
Synthesize the story as a team communication breakdown and ask how that affects them.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option B is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 6 (Listens Actively), which includes integrating and summarizing information succinctly without adding interpretation to help the client gain clarity. Synthesizing key threads and checking what matters most brings focus back to the client's priorities. Option A is clearly wrong because soliciting more third-party backstory pulls the session further into external storytelling rather than client clarity. Option C is a tricky distractor that appears disciplined around Competency 3 session management, yet redirects abruptly without first demonstrating active listening or helping the client distill what they shared. Option D is a tricky distractor that sounds like synthesis, yet adds the coach's diagnostic label ('team communication breakdown').

mock_exam_batch.competency_reference: Core Competency 7: Evokes Awareness
mock_exam_batch.scenario_question: A client states firmly, "No matter how hard I work, executives will never promote someone from operations." What is the BEST response for the coach?

options.text: Confirm that breaking out of operations is tough and suggest exploring external job opportunities.
Ask how increasing visibility with senior leaders might alter their view of operations staff.
Ask for factual proof that nobody from operations has ever earned an executive promotion.
Invite the client to question that assumption by considering other possible workplace perspectives.

ai_rationale.explanation: Option D is correct under 2025 ICF Core Competency 7 (Evokes Awareness). When a client expresses an absolute limiting belief, the coach gently invites examination of the assumption and opens space for broader perspectives without debating or imposing answers. Option A is clearly wrong because treating the client's belief as settled fact and suggesting job-hunting undermines awareness and inserts advice.
